title: AI Foundations Capstone
summary: Plan, execute, verify, and explain a complete AI-assisted workflow with evidence that another person can review.
objectives: Select a useful, bounded objective and identify data and authority limits.
Create a reproducible prompt or workflow plan with acceptance criteria.
Collect source, tool, output, and verification evidence.
Recover from a meaningful failure or document a tested recovery path.
Present the result and reflect on correctness, evidence, safety, reproducibility, and communication.

activity.title: Complete an evidence-based AI workflow
instructions: Choose a low-risk research, writing, coding, analysis, or tool-use task and complete the objective brief.
Create and execute a prompt or workflow plan with source, data, authority, checkpoint, and recovery boundaries.
Preserve the required artifacts without secrets or unnecessary personal information.
Verify every acceptance criterion independently and record a real or safely simulated failure-and-recovery cycle.
Prepare a concise handoff, score each rubric criterion with evidence, and write the reflection.
activity.reflectionPrompt: What changed between your initial plan and the verified result, and what evidence justified that change?

capstone.title: Evidence-based practical AI workflow
capstone.summary: Demonstrate a complete, safe, reproducible AI-assisted workflow and submit traceable evidence for review.

criteria.title: Correctness
criteria.description: The deliverable satisfies the stated objective and acceptance criteria, with limitations identified.

criteria.title: Evidence
criteria.description: Material claims and decisions are traceable to authoritative sources, tool results, or direct observations.

criteria.title: Safety
criteria.description: Data, permissions, approvals, and consequential actions stay inside explicit boundaries.

criteria.title: Reproducibility
criteria.description: Another person can repeat the workflow and understand how failure was detected and recovered.

criteria.title: Communication
criteria.description: The handoff clearly separates facts, generated suggestions, decisions, uncertainty, and next steps.

cues.text: Introduce the capstone as evidence of a bounded workflow, not a contest for the most impressive output.
Reveal the objective brief from user need through acceptance criteria, data boundary, authority, and scope.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static objective brief lists user and need, deliverable, acceptance criteria, allowed data, authority, and excluded scope. Reduced-motion mode shows the complete list.

cues.text: Connect prompt structure, trusted context, output contracts, checkpoints, and failure behavior into one workflow plan.
Ask learners to name the first condition that would make them stop their workflow.
Allow three minutes to complete scope, data, and authority boundaries.
Demonstrate an evidence log that preserves reproducibility without preserving secrets or hidden reasoning.
Show independent checks and one failure-and-recovery record tied to acceptance criteria.
Walk through the five-part rubric and show how a reviewer traces each awarded point to evidence.
Check that every learner can identify five artifacts, five rubric criteria, and the eighty-percent threshold.
Guide learners through execution, evidence capture, self-review, and preparation for an independent reviewer.
Begin the knowledge check, then collect the scored capstone evidence and reflection.

questions.prompt: What makes a task suitable for this capstone?
choices: It has the largest possible impact
It is bounded, low-risk, useful, and produces reviewable evidence
questions.explanation: The capstone assesses a complete workflow, so the task must be safe to execute and possible to verify.

choices: The exact plan, material inputs, versions, checks, and recovery record
A statement that the output looked good
questions.explanation: Reproducibility needs a traceable procedure and observable evidence without hidden reasoning or secrets.

questions.prompt: How should a capstone verify an AI-generated factual claim?
choices: Use an authoritative source or direct test appropriate to the claim
questions.explanation: Independent, claim-appropriate evidence is stronger than model self-confirmation.

questions.prompt: What must be included when no real failure occurs?
choices: A safely simulated likely failure with stop, recovery, and verification behavior
questions.explanation: A safe simulation can demonstrate recovery competence without creating harmful real-world failure.

questions.prompt: When is the capstone module complete?
choices: After passing only the knowledge check
After passing both the knowledge check and the scored capstone rubric
questions.explanation: Both knowledge and applied evidence are required for completion.
